title: Review: Photons and the photoelectric effect; Wave–particle duality; Temperature, internal energy, thermal equilibrium; Specific heat capacity and latent heat; Gas laws and ideal gas equation; Kinetic theory of gases
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: T01-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; T01-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; Q01-1#t4 term and clue written for the game; T01-1#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: Q01-1#N.13, T01-1#N.7, T02-1#N.9, T05-1#N.9a, T01-1#N.9a, T02-1#N.10, T05-1#N.12, T01-1#N.11.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Thermal equilibrium
items.clue: Condition of bodies in contact with no net energy transfer between them.

items.label: Temperature
items.clue: Property that decides which way net energy flows between two bodies in contact.

items.label: Planck constant
items.clue: Symbol h: the energy of one quantum of light divided by its f; 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.

items.label: Internal energy
items.clue: Total of the random kinetic and potential contributions of all the particles in a body.

questions.stem: Light whose photons each have energy 4.0 eV shines on three metals: X, with work function 2.0 eV; Y, with work function 3.0 eV; and Z, with work function 4.5 eV. Which statement about the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons emitted from each metal is correct?

options.text: Z's electrons have the greatest maximum kinetic energy, and X's electrons the least
X's electrons have the greatest maximum kinetic energy, and Z emits no electrons
All three metals emit electrons, each with the same maximum kinetic energy
Their maximum kinetic energies cannot be ranked without the light's intensity

questions.stem: A pure substance is heated steadily from a solid until it has completely boiled. According to the molecular model, which statement about its molecules is correct?

options.text: Their mean separation increases greatly on melting and increases again on boiling.
Their mean separation changes little on melting but increases greatly on boiling.
The molecules themselves get larger on melting, and larger again on boiling.
The molecules start to move only on melting, and they move faster still on boiling.

questions.stem: 0.40 kg of ice at 0 °C is melted and the water is then warmed to 20 °C. Specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹; specific latent heat of vaporisation of water = 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹; specific heat capacity of water = 4.18 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. What is the total energy that must be supplied?

A bubble of gas of volume 2.0 cm³ is released at the bottom of a lake, where the pressure is 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa and the temperature is 7 °C. It rises to the surface, where the pressure is 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and the temperature is 17 °C. Treat the gas as ideal, with no gas gained or lost. What is its volume at the surface?

options.text: 6.0 cm³
15 cm³
6.2 cm³
0.69 cm³

questions.explanation: pressure × volume ÷ T is constant: V₂ = 2.0 × (3.0 × 10⁵/1.0 × 10⁵) × (290/280) = 6.2 cm³.

questions.stem: You have 1.0 kg of ice at 0 °C and 1.0 kg of liquid water at 0 °C. Which statement about their internal energies is correct?

options.text: They are equal, since both are at the same temperature.
The water has more: its molecules have more potential energy.
The ice has more, since strong forces hold its molecules in place.
The water has more, since its molecules move faster on average.

questions.explanation: Melting takes in energy with no rise in temperature. That energy separates the molecules, raising their potential energy; their mean kinetic energy is unchanged.

questions.stem: 0.20 kg of water and 0.20 kg of cooking oil, both at 20 °C, are each supplied with 12 kJ of energy. Specific heat capacities: water 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, oil 2000 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Assume no energy is lost. Which statement about their final temperatures is correct?

options.text: The oil ends at 50 °C and the water at about 34 °C.
The water ends at 50 °C and the oil at about 34 °C.
They end at the same temperature, as each gets 12 kJ.
The oil ends at 30 °C and the water at about 14 °C.

questions.stem: A sealed, rigid container holds an ideal gas at 7 °C. The gas is heated to 287 °C. How does its new pressure compare with its starting pressure?

options.text: It is the same, because the container is rigid, so the volume cannot change.
It is 41 times as large, because the temperature has risen from 7 °C to 287 °C.
It is twice as large, because the absolute temperature doubles, from 280 K to 560 K.
It is 1.4 times as large, because the molecules move √2 times as fast.

questions.explanation: At constant volume, pressure ÷ absolute temperature is constant. 560 K/280 K = 2.

questions.stem: A thermometer at room temperature, 20 °C, is placed in a cup of water at 70 °C. Its reading rises for a while and then stays steady. Why does the steady reading give the temperature of the water?

options.text: All energy transfer between the thermometer and the water has then stopped completely for good.
The thermometer then has as much internal energy as the water in the cup, so the two readings match.
The cold in the thermometer has then all flowed out into the water, so it can read correctly.
They are then in thermal equilibrium, so no net energy is transferred between them.
